title: 6.1: Introduction to Web Technologies: HTML & CSS
summary: This chapter introduces the fundamental web technologies HTML and CSS. You'll learn how HTML provides the structure and content of web pages using tags and attributes, and how CSS is used to style these pages, controlling layout, colors, and fonts. We'll cover the core syntax of both languages, explore different methods for integrating CSS, and delve into the crucial CSS Box Model for element positioning. The chapter concludes with hands-on activities to build and style a simple profile page, solidifying your understanding of these foundational front-end development skills.

HTML, or HyperText Markup Language, is the backbone of the web. Think of it as the skeleton and organs of a webpage, defining its structure and content. It's a markup language that uses special keywords called tags, like `

This is a paragraph.

`. Some tags, like `` for images, are self-closing. Every HTML document starts with `` to declare its type, followed by the root `` element. Inside ``, you'll find two main sections: ``, which holds metadata like the page title and links to stylesheets, and ``, which contains all the visible content you see in your browser. This includes all your headings, paragraphs, images, and links. Elements often have attributes, like `href` for links or `src` for images, which provide extra information. A common pitfall for beginners is forgetting to close tags or nesting them incorrectly, leading to unexpected display issues. screens.narration_script: Once you have your webpage's structure defined with HTML, you'll want to make it visually appealing. That's where CSS, or Cascading Style Sheets, comes in. CSS is like the skin and clothing of our webpage body; it dictates the visual presentation—things like colors, fonts, spacing, and overall layout. Without CSS, even a perfectly structured HTML page would appear as plain, unformatted text. A core principle of good web design is separating content, which is HTML, from its presentation, which is CSS. This makes your code cleaner, easier to maintain, and much more flexible. CSS rules are made up of two main parts: a selector and a declaration block. The selector targets the specific HTML element or elements you want to style, for example, `h1` to target all `<h1>` tags. The declaration block then contains one or more declarations, each specifying a property, like `color` or `font-size`, and its corresponding value, such as `navy` or `2em`. So, a rule like `h1 { color: navy; font-size: 2em; }` would select all `<h1>` elements and set their text color to navy and their font size to twice the default.
delivery_notes: Use the 'skin and clothing' analogy for CSS.
Emphasize separation of concerns.
Break down the CSS rule structure clearly.

segment_breaks.text: There are three primary ways to incorporate CSS into your HTML document, each with its own use cases. First, we have **inline CSS**, where you apply styles directly to an HTML element using its `style` attribute.

For example, `

This text is red.

`. While simple for quick changes, it mixes content and presentation, making it generally discouraged for larger projects due to poor maintainability.

Next is **internal CSS**, where you place your CSS rules within a `<style>` tag located inside the `<head>` section of your HTML document. This method is suitable for single pages or when styles are unique to that specific page.

Finally, the most recommended and scalable method is **external CSS**. Here, you write all your CSS in a separate `.css` file and link it to your HTML document using a `<link>` tag in the `<head>` section, like `<link rel='stylesheet' href='styles.css'>`. This approach keeps your HTML clean, promotes reusability of styles across multiple pages, and makes your project much easier to manage and update.

screens.narration_script: A crucial concept in CSS for controlling layout and spacing is the **box model**. The browser treats every HTML element on a webpage as a rectangular box. This box isn't just the content you see; it's composed of four distinct layers, working from the inside out. At the very center is the **content** itself—your text, images, or other elements. Surrounding the content is **padding**, which provides internal space between the content and the element's border. Think of it as cushioning. Next, we have the **border**, a visible line that wraps around both the content and its padding. This border can have various styles, widths, and colors. Finally, on the outermost layer, is the **margin**. This creates external space around the entire element, separating it from other elements on the page. Understanding these components is vital because `width` and `height` properties typically refer only to the content area. Padding, border, and margin are *added* on top of that, which can sometimes lead to unexpected element sizes. A common solution to this is `box-sizing: border-box;`, which alters the calculation so that `width` and `height` include the padding and border. Mastering the box model will help you precisely control the layout and spacing of all elements on your web pages.
delivery_notes: Explain each layer of the box model clearly.
Use the 'cushioning' analogy for padding.
Emphasize the default calculation of width/height.
Introduce `box-sizing: border-box;` as a solution.
